evidence.observation: Entry point: POST /auth/refresh handler. Both InvalidToken AND TokenReuseDetected result in 401 + cleared cookie. No distinction shown to the user — both paths produce a silent logout.

Non-atomic read-check-write: (1) findByHash at line 52, (2) revoked_at check at line 56, (3) revoke at line 60, (4) insert at line 64. Between steps 1 and 3 another concurrent request can read the same unrevoked token.

Reuse detection: if a token already has revoked_at != null, the whole family is nuked and TokenReuseDetected is thrown. In the concurrent scenario, request-2 reaches this point AFTER request-1 set revoked_at via repo.revoke(), triggering a false positive.
Plain SELECT with no transaction isolation. Two concurrent requests can both call this and both receive a row with revoked_at=NULL.
Standalone UPDATE, not inside a transaction wrapping the whole rotate() sequence.

hypotheses.statement: Two concurrent POST /auth/refresh requests with the same rt cookie both execute rotate(). Both call findByHash() before either calls revoke(). Both read row.revoked_at=NULL. Request-1 calls revoke() first. Request-2 then reads the token AGAIN via the stale in-memory row from step 1, reaches the row.revoked_at check (line 56) — which is now non-null in the DB — and triggers revokeFamily() → the newly issued token from request-1 is also revoked → 401.
hypotheses.experiment: Call rotate() twice concurrently with the same token; assert the new token from the successful call is still valid (i.e. isFamilyRevoked returns false) after both calls complete.

hypotheses.statement: The rotate() function lacks a database transaction, which means the read-check-write is not atomic. Wrapping all operations in a single IMMEDIATE transaction would force request-2 to wait and then find the token already revoked, throwing InvalidToken (not TokenReuseDetected), preserving the family.
hypotheses.experiment: Wrap the body of rotate() in db.transaction(). Run the concurrent repro test. Confirm the repro test passes.
